Nonverbal Dominance.short_definition: Using posture, stares, sighs, eye rolls or the way a body fills a room to dismiss or pressure someone without saying anything.
Nonverbal Dominance.core_meaning: Using posture, stares, sighs, eye rolls or the way a body fills a room to dismiss or pressure someone without saying anything.
Nonverbal Dominance.expanded_definition: Nonverbal dominance is pressure carried by the body instead of words. Examples are a pointed sigh, an eye roll, a long stare, or standing over someone who is seated. Another is taking the head of the table and more room than the moment needs. When it is mostly about how someone stands or sits, it is called postural dominance. Each signal is easy to deny and hard to quote. One sigh means little. It is a concern when it reliably lands on moments when you disagree, correct something or ask for something. You may start editing yourself around it.
Nonverbal Dominance.plain_language_summary: Without saying a word, someone uses sighs, stares, eye rolls or where they stand to make you feel small, so you stop disagreeing. There is nothing you could quote back to them.
Nonverbal Dominance.why_this_matters: Nothing quotable is said, so the experience is hard to explain to anyone else. You may end up quietly editing yourself around a reaction you could not describe if asked. Being looked down on, literally, works below the level of argument. You feel smaller and cannot point to why.
what_it_is: Signals sent with the face and body. They include sighs, eye rolls, long stares and a turned back. Another is a slow exhale timed to the end of your sentence.
Positioning that puts you lower or smaller. Examples are standing over you while you sit, taking the head of the table, or leaning over your desk or your chair.
Wordless, so it leaves nothing to quote and is easy to answer with 'I didn't say anything.'
Found in kitchens, meetings, classrooms and car rides, where the same sigh can carry a very different weight.
What sets it apart from ordinary body language is aim. It lands on disagreement, correction or a request, and not on everything that irritates the person.
what_it_sounds_like: A long exhale and an eye roll the moment you say 'I see it differently', and none when you agree.
They stay standing at the counter looking down at you while you explain, and only sit once you stop talking.
Silent staring after you ask for something, held until you say 'never mind'.
You raise a concern in a meeting and a manager leans back with arms folded, eyes on the ceiling, while others speak without that reaction.
When you correct a detail they step closer or lean over your chair.
They turn away or pick up a phone as soon as you mention the budget.
You ask what is wrong and hear: 'Nothing. I didn't say anything.'
what_it_is_not: Faces move on their own: a flash of visible irritation, an expressive manner, a real sigh at the end of a long day. Ask whether the reaction appears whenever something is annoying, or only when one person disagrees.
Rooms have layouts. A standing desk, a low sofa or a narrow kitchen can put one person above another. Someone standing up is usually just about to leave.
People differ in height, build and posture, and a tall or broad person takes up room without meaning anything by it.
A family or cultural style of long or short eye contact, or comfortable silence, that shows up with everyone.
Tiredness, pain, or a neurological or sensory difference that shapes facial expression and eye contact.
A frown or far-off stare while someone concentrates on what you are saying.
this_may_be_it_when: The sigh, stare or positioning follows disagreement, correction or a request far more often than anything else.
It stops or softens when you give in or go quiet.
Other people in the same room get a different reaction when they say the same thing.
Your body reacts first, by shrinking, going quiet or tightening, before you can say what happened.
If you ask about it, you hear a denial with no other explanation, and the same signal returns next time.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The same expressions show up with everyone, including people with more power than you.
A plain spoken reason comes when you ask, such as 'Sorry, my back hurts, I can't sit.'
It belongs to a hard season, like grief or illness, and eases as that passes.
The positioning is dictated by the room, such as the only free seat or the person nearest the screen.
You can say 'I disagree' and the person engages with what you said.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Chronic pain, a bad night's sleep or a long shift can come out as sighs, frowns and refusing to sit.
Some people sigh to release tension and barely know they are doing it.
Norms about eye contact, personal space and who stands differ across cultures and families. The same stare can mean something else where the person grew up.
A resting face can look stern or contemptuous when nothing is meant.
common_false_positives: A colleague who stands to talk because they think better on their feet.
A teenager's eye roll that is mostly mood and appears with everyone at home.
Someone who is visibly frustrated by a slow website, a stuck printer and then a disagreement, in the same way each time.
discernment_questions: Does the reaction come when I disagree, ask or correct, or whenever the person is annoyed about anything?
Do I change what I say, or whether I speak, because of it?
Do other people get the same reaction when they say the same thing?
If someone I trust had watched the same exchange, would they describe the body language the way I do?
Do I feel dismissed, or do I feel afraid?
less_concerning_if: It appears with everyone and in every sort of mood, whether or not you disagree.
The person is open when told how a particular look landed, and it changes.
You can still say what you think and be heard after the sigh.
more_concerning_if: The stares and looming come with raised voices, blocked doorways or damage to objects.
It travels with spoken put-downs, monitoring or control of money, so the silence is one part of a larger pattern.
You have stopped raising some subjects altogether because of the reaction you expect.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start sentences with 'sorry' or shrink them before they react.
The subjects that draw the reaction slowly drop off the list of things you bring up.
You read their face and posture as you walk in to work out what kind of evening it will be.
Described aloud to friends, the sigh sounds trivial, which leaves you doubting yourself.
Nonverbal Dominance.repair_check: Repair shows up in the body as well as in a sentence. Look for whether the sighs and looming ease when you disagree. Look too for whether the person can say what the look meant and why it was unfair. An apology followed by the same stare next week has changed nothing.
Nonverbal Dominance.boundary_respect_check: After you say you would rather hear what they think than guess from a look, what do you see over the next days? It might be words, a quieter version of the same look, or a silence that seems to punish you for asking.
Nonverbal Dominance.psychological_mechanism: People read faces and posture quickly, below conscious thought. Many learn early to treat a frown or a looming figure as a cue to back down. A wordless signal gives you no statement to argue with, so the response happens in the body first. Over repeated moments, a person can start editing themselves before anything is said.
Nonverbal Dominance.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe going quiet in the room, rehearsing sentences, shrinking in their chair, and feeling tense before they have said anything. Some say they cannot explain to others why a sigh frightens them, and begin to wonder if they are oversensitive. Others describe losing the habit of disagreeing at all.

response_options.soft_clarification: Pick a calm moment and ask for words: 'I can't always tell what that look means. Can you tell me what you think?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Describe the effect on you once. Do not ask for a promise. You could say: 'When I get a stare after I speak, I stop saying what I think. I would like to hear it in words.'
response_options.disengagement: Choose where you sit and stand so you are level with the person, near a door and, where you can, in view of others. Keep harder subjects for times when someone else is around.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe what you see, and how your body reacts, to a trusted person or a domestic violence advocate. Ask if it sounds like part of something larger, especially if you feel afraid.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down dates, who was present and what you saw, in plain description ('stood over my desk while I spoke, arms folded'). Ask for meetings to run with an agenda or a third person present.

Nonverbal Dominance.boundary_script: "I can't always tell what a look means, and I would like to hear what you think in words. Could we sit down and each say our piece?"
Nonverbal Dominance.safety_note: Stares, looming and slow exhales weigh more when they sit beside shouting, broken objects, blocked doorways or being followed from room to room. Then the body language can be a reminder of what has happened before. If you fear the person's reaction, avoid confronting the signals directly. Write down each incident with the date and bring the list to a domestic violence advocate before changing how you respond.
misuse_warning: Reading contempt into every sigh turns ordinary tiredness into an attack. A look is ambiguous; the label needs a repeated link to your disagreement, not one frown.
Accusing someone of dominating a room because of their height or build turns a body into a charge. The pattern is the timing around disagreement, not the body itself.
Nonverbal Dominance.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Spatial Invasion uses closeness itself, such as cornering, blocking an exit or removing personal space, so the body is the barrier. Nonverbal dominance can work from across a room, through a sigh or a stare. Emotion Control governs which feelings you are allowed to show, using shame, reward and punishment, and is often spoken. The silent signal here is aimed at your disagreement, not at your feelings.

Fabricated Evidence.short_definition: Passing off invented or altered messages, images or documents as genuine proof of something that did not happen or was not said.
Fabricated Evidence.core_meaning: Passing off invented or altered messages, images or documents as genuine proof of something that did not happen or was not said.
Fabricated Evidence.expanded_definition: Fabricated evidence is material that looks like a record but is not one. Examples are an edited message thread, a screenshot of a conversation that never took place, a changed date or a forged document. These are offered as proof. Many people know it as forged screenshots, since a faked image of a message is the most common kind. Screenshots are often treated as settled proof, which is why a fake can carry weight. It differs from a real record taken out of context, because here the item itself is not authentic. It is usually shown to a third party, so the harm falls on your credibility.
Fabricated Evidence.plain_language_summary: Someone shows others a screenshot or document that looks real but was made up or changed. They present it as proof of something you never wrote, said or did.
Fabricated Evidence.why_this_matters: Screenshots and documents are widely accepted as proof. Disproving a fake means asking people to doubt evidence they normally trust. Meanwhile your own account can start to look like the lie. The harm can reach work, school or court before anyone checks the item.
what_it_is: A message, image or document that looks like a record but was edited, put together or invented, then presented as real.
It is either a full invention, such as a conversation that never took place, or a change to something real. The change might be a different word, name, date or amount.
Usually shown to a third party, such as friends, an employer, a school, a platform or a court, and not to you.
Often introduced with a phrase like 'I have receipts'. That asks for trust in how the thing looks, and not in what it contains.
Found in breakups, custody fights, workplace disputes, online feuds and disputes with institutions. It shows up wherever a record could decide whose account is believed.
It concerns whether the record itself is genuine, which is different from whether someone remembers events correctly.
what_it_sounds_like: 'Here are the receipts', followed by a screenshot of words you have no memory of writing.
A thread shown to your employer or friends that does not match the same conversation on your own phone.
A message under your name, with phrasing or punctuation you never use.
Timestamps, contact names or dates that do not fit when you were actually in touch, or an app layout that does not match the app it claims to come from.
A screenshot with no way to see the surrounding messages, and a refusal to produce the original phone or an export.
A document that cites an agreement, policy or payment you have never seen or signed.
'I don't need to show you the original. The picture says it all.'
what_it_is_not: A real screenshot cropped for brevity, with its meaning intact. Cropping is not forging.
Confusion about which conversation or time frame an image comes from. People mix up threads constantly.
Authentic images that look different because of another device, language setting or app update.
A genuine message quoted out of context. That can mislead, but the record itself is real, which is a different problem from invented content.
A sincere misremembering of what was written, from someone who shows what they honestly believe the message said.
A real record with a phone number or name blacked out for privacy, labeled as such, with the rest untouched.
this_may_be_it_when: The record contradicts your own copy of the same conversation in wording, order or dates.
The phrasing is unlike your own, or it mentions events you never took part in.
Only an image is offered, never the original device, account export or file.
Neither the platform nor anyone else can match the item to a real message.
The item appears just as a decision is being made about you, such as a hearing, review or breakup.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Your own copy of the thread, once you look, matches it.
The difference is a cropped section or a missing earlier message, not changed words.
The platform's own export confirms the messages and dates.
The person who sent it also shares the original and invites you to compare.
The odd formatting is explained by a different phone, language setting or app version.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Memory of an old exchange is often worse than people expect, and a real thread can surprise the person who wrote it.
Messages can come from an old or shared account or device and be forgotten.
Someone who received a forwarded screenshot may repeat it, believing it genuine.
Apps display the same message differently across devices, time zones and language settings.
common_false_positives: A screenshot that looks wrong only because it is cropped on a small screen.
A real message you sent while upset or tired and no longer recall.
A document retyped or reformatted to fit a form, with the same content.
discernment_questions: Do I have my own copy of the same conversation, and does it match word for word?
Can the original be checked on the device, account or platform it is said to come from?
Do the names, times and layout fit the app and the date claimed?
Does the wording sound like how I write, and does it mention things I could not have known?
Who is the item being shown to, and what decision is it meant to influence?
Was anyone else in this conversation who could confirm it?
less_concerning_if: The original can be opened and checked, and it matches what you were shown.
The person corrects the record when shown your copy.
The disagreement is about what a real message meant, not whether it was written.
more_concerning_if: The item is used in a formal complaint, or in a custody or protective-order matter. Or it is used to get you dismissed or shut out of a group.
More than one doubtful item has appeared, or accounts that hold the originals have become unavailable to you.
The other person has had access to your phone, accounts or cloud backups.
pattern_over_time_signs: More than one doubtful item appears, each shown to a different audience.
Records that could settle the matter, such as old messages, vanish or become unavailable.
Your standing with mutual friends, a workplace or a school drops without your knowing what was said.
You begin exporting or photographing your own conversations regularly to protect yourself.
Fabricated Evidence.repair_check: Correction here looks like paperwork. The item is withdrawn from everyone who saw it, the original is produced and compared, and the audience is told it was not genuine. An apology to you alone, while the fake stays in circulation, leaves the damage where it was.
Fabricated Evidence.boundary_respect_check: Ask in writing, calmly, to see the original. Does it appear, can a neutral person examine it, or does the talk move to how you reacted? Whether the item can be examined is the test, not how confident anyone sounds.
Fabricated Evidence.psychological_mechanism: A record-shaped object earns trust quickly, and a screenshot has the air of a witness who cannot be argued with. Third parties often have no way to check it, so the first version they see can set their view. The person it targets may start doubting their own memory, which can make the fake feel more believable.
Fabricated Evidence.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe shock at reading words attributed to them, then a scramble to prove a negative. Some lose standing at work, with friends or in a legal matter before anyone checks the item. Others describe doubting their memory, going silent to avoid more material, and feeling that being believed has turned into a technical problem.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask to see the record in the app it came from, not as an image. Try: 'Can we open that conversation on the phone it came from?' A genuine record can usually survive that request.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue about the item with the person who produced it. Move the question to a neutral reviewer, such as a platform, a mediator or HR, who can compare originals.
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying about the item, delete nothing on your side, and do not repost the fake to disprove it, since that spreads it further. Save it with its source and date.
response_options.support_seeking: Bring your saved originals and the suspect item to a lawyer, legal aid clinic or victim services advocate. Ask how originals are authenticated.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If it reached your employer or school, give HR or the conduct office your own export with dates. Ask in writing that the item be checked against originals before anything is decided.

Fabricated Evidence.boundary_script: "That does not match my records of this conversation. I have the original with its dates saved, and I'd ask that whoever decides this look at both side by side before drawing a conclusion."
Fabricated Evidence.safety_note: A fabricated record may be used in a custody dispute, a protective-order hearing, a workplace complaint or a threat of exposure. It can cost you housing, income, children or safety, so treat it as a legal matter and not as an argument. Save originals with their dates, delete nothing, and speak to a lawyer or legal aid before replying to the person who produced it. If you fear for your safety, an advocate can help you plan.
misuse_warning: Calling a damaging screenshot fake is the same move reversed: a real record can be disowned with the word 'forged'. Ask for the original, not a verdict.
Telling others that a named person forged something, without evidence, is itself an accusation. Describe which details do not match instead.
Fabricated Evidence.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Fabricated evidence is a false object that borrows the authority of a record, so it can be passed to others and outlive the conversation. Lying is a false statement in someone's own voice. Lying by Omission invents nothing and leaves out a piece of a true story. Vague Allegations point to unnamed critics or unspecified accusations with nothing to inspect. Fabricated evidence gives you something concrete to inspect that turns out not to be authentic.

Half-Truth Framing.short_definition: Choosing and arranging statements that are each true so that the listener ends up with a false overall picture.
Half-Truth Framing.core_meaning: Choosing and arranging statements that are each true so that the listener ends up with a false overall picture.
Half-Truth Framing.expanded_definition: Half-truth framing builds a false impression out of true statements. Each sentence holds up when checked. The pieces are picked and ordered so the listener reaches a conclusion the full facts would not support. The word paltering means the same thing. It often shows up as a technically accurate answer to a direct question, followed by 'everything I said was true'. One hurried summary proves little. It is a concern when answers keep steering the same way on the same kind of topic.
Half-Truth Framing.plain_language_summary: Everything said is true, yet you walk away believing something that is not. Each fact checks out, so the problem only shows when you see what was left around it.
Half-Truth Framing.why_this_matters: Every fact checks out, so even a careful listener who verifies still ends up with the wrong conclusion. When you object, you are told, correctly, that nothing false was said. That can leave you doubting your own reasonable guess instead of the account.
what_it_is: A set of true statements, chosen and ordered so that they imply something the whole story would not support.
Often a true answer to a slightly different question than the one asked.
Works because most people assume a truthful answer is an honest one, and rarely check what sits around it.
This is different from an outright lie, because every sentence can be defended. It is also different from plain omission, because the pieces are fitted together to point somewhere.
Found in sales pitches, job references, relationship disputes, apologies and reports to bosses.
what_it_sounds_like: 'Did the repair pass inspection?' / 'The inspector spent an hour at the house.'
'Were you out with anyone last night?' / 'I was at the pub until eleven.' (the question was who)
'But everything I said was true.' offered after you discover the gap.
'The company has never missed a payroll.' (said of a firm about to close)
'I never told her she was fired. I only said her role was changing.'
'Sales are up 20 percent this month.' (after a 40 percent drop the month before, left unsaid)
Asked a direct question, they answer fully and warmly, about something next to it.
what_it_is_not: An accurate summary necessarily omits detail for length.
People often present facts in whatever order those facts occurred to them, with no steer in mind.
A genuinely different, honestly held interpretation of the same true facts is disagreement rather than arrangement.
Careful, precise people answer exactly what was asked and nothing more. That can sound evasive without steering anyone anywhere.
An honest answer given with an incomplete picture, because that was all the speaker had.
Things people have a right to keep private, such as medical history, when they say it is private and do not imply something else.
this_may_be_it_when: The answer addresses a neighboring question, not the one you asked.
When the missing context is added, the impression it created falls apart.
Challenging the impression gets 'but everything I said was true' and no acknowledgment of what you were led to believe.
It shows up on topics where the full picture would cost the speaker something.
A plain yes or no was available, and a longer answer was given instead, again and again.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Adding the missing context leaves the picture unchanged.
They accept 'that's not what I understood' and fill in the rest without being pressed.
The same wordy, precise style shows up on every topic, including ones with nothing at stake.
The speaker did not know the full picture themselves.
You were told the limits at the start: 'I can only speak to this part.'
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Nervous speakers often answer a nearby question because they are rushing to say something.
Professional training in saying only what is certain can make answers sound slippery.
Some people fear a plain 'no' will start a fight, and soften it with true but beside-the-point detail.
Asked in a hurry, people give the first true thing that comes to mind.
common_false_positives: A friend telling a story in the order it happened, with the ending last.
A status report that stresses good news because it was asked to be brief.
A witness who answers a narrowly worded question narrowly.
discernment_questions: If I put the full set of facts in front of a neutral person, would they reach the conclusion I was led to?
Was the question I asked answered, or a nearby one?
Was there a plain, still-honest way to answer that was not used?
When I add what was missing, does the person take it on board or resist?
Does this show up only on subjects where the full picture is inconvenient?
less_concerning_if: The person fills in the missing context as soon as you ask.
The slanted account came from a hurried summary and not from a conversation about something that mattered.
The impression was minor, and correcting it costs neither side anything.
more_concerning_if: You made a decision, such as signing, paying or staying, on the strength of the impression.
The same kind of answer keeps coming about money, whereabouts or health.
When you check the facts, you are told you should have asked more precisely.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself asking questions in more and more exact wording to get a straight answer.
You learn what the gaps were later, from other people and not from them.
'Technically true' becomes a phrase you hear from them, or say about them.
You trust their literal words less while still being unable to point to a lie.
Half-Truth Framing.repair_check: Repair starts with the person saying what picture they let you form and what they knew that would have changed it. Then they offer the rest without being asked. Watch whether later answers to direct questions get plainer. An apology that defends every sentence as true has repaired nothing.
Half-Truth Framing.boundary_respect_check: Ask a question that has only one honest short answer and notice what comes back. A yes or a no, even an unwelcome one, shows the request was heard. Another accurate but roundabout reply shows the old shape returning.
Half-Truth Framing.psychological_mechanism: Listeners tend to assume a speaker is being cooperative, so they fill gaps with the most natural meaning of what they hear. True statements pass the checks people normally run, which leaves the false conclusion as the listener's own inference. That can make a complaint harder, because the speaker can truthfully say that every sentence was accurate.
Half-Truth Framing.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some feel foolish for believing something that was never technically said, and are unable to explain the complaint to others. They may begin to cross-examine every answer, or blame themselves for not asking the right question. Some describe losing the sense that plain conversation with this person is possible.

response_options.soft_clarification: Restate the answer you were given and ask the one thing it left open: 'That's true, but it doesn't tell me whether you went. Did you?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say you want direct answers to direct questions on this topic, and that 'technically true' will not do. For example: 'When I ask yes or no, I need yes or no.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to corner the person with sharper wording. Get the facts from the original source, such as the document, the account or a third party, and let the conversation go.
response_options.support_seeking: Lay out the exchange to someone neutral and ask what conclusion they would draw from what was said. It checks whether your inference was reasonable.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In writing, ask for confirmation of the specific facts you need ('Please confirm whether the contract includes overtime') and keep the reply. A written yes or no is harder to blur.

Half-Truth Framing.boundary_script: "Thank you, I believe what you told me is accurate. I'd still like a plain yes or no to my question: did it happen or not? I make decisions based on the picture I'm left with, so I need the whole picture."
Half-Truth Framing.safety_note: A misleading frame made of true parts is a communication problem, not a danger signal. That changes if the missing piece is about safety, money, a health risk or custody. It also changes if asking questions brings anger or payback. In those cases, check the facts through documents or an independent source before you act. Take the matter to a lawyer, advisor or doctor instead of relying on the person's own account.
misuse_warning: Calling any careful or incomplete answer a half-truth treats privacy and precision as lies. The label needs a gap between the impression left and the facts, shown with the facts.
'Technically true' can be thrown at someone to win an argument about interpretation. If both readings fit the facts, it is a disagreement.
Half-Truth Framing.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying states something false. Half-truth framing states nothing false and acts through what is picked and in what order. Lying by Omission is a gap, a fact left out of an otherwise complete account. Here, the stated facts are fitted together to point at a conclusion. Frame Control decides the subject and terms of a conversation. A half-truth can sit inside any frame, as long as the facts told lead somewhere the whole would not.

Lying by Omission.short_definition: Leaving out information the other person needs for an accurate picture, while everything that is said stays technically true.
Lying by Omission.core_meaning: Leaving out information the other person needs for an accurate picture, while everything that is said stays technically true.
Lying by Omission.expanded_definition: Lying by omission is a true account with the important piece missing. What is said holds up; the gap is where the false picture forms. Gaslighting by omission and selective information sharing are other ways of naming it. Sometimes the missing piece is a single fact, sometimes it is a steady filtering of which facts one person gets. One forgotten detail means little. It is a concern when the missing pieces are the ones that would have changed your decision, and they keep being missing.
Lying by Omission.plain_language_summary: You are told true things, but not the one fact that would have changed what you decided. You find out later, from someone else or by accident, that it was known all along.
Lying by Omission.why_this_matters: Nothing said was false, so there is no untruth to point at. There is only a conclusion you reached on grounds you did not know were incomplete. The missing piece usually appears too late to change what you chose. You may blame yourself for not asking.
what_it_is: An account that is accurate in every sentence, with the one piece that would change its meaning absent.
Can be a single missing fact, such as a debt or a diagnosis, or an ongoing filter on which facts reach you.
Often found by chance, from a letter, a third person or a record, not from the person who knew.
Sometimes the information was mentioned in a way that buried it. An example is a passing remark in an unrelated conversation that later counts as 'I told you.'
Matters most where the listener is deciding something, such as signing, buying, moving, lending or trusting.
What separates privacy from concealment is whether the other person is relying on the incomplete picture to make a decision.
what_it_sounds_like: 'I never said that wasn't true.'
'I told you about it.' (a passing remark, months ago, in a different conversation)
'You never asked.'
'It didn't seem relevant.' (said about the one detail the decision turned on)
A version of a story that includes everything favoring one side and nothing that complicates it.
'Why would I bring that up? It wasn't your business.' (after you had to deal with its effects)
You learn from someone else a fact they had known all along and never mentioned.
what_it_is_not: Not thinking to mention something that did not seem relevant at the time is ordinary.
Plenty of information is nobody else's business. A friend's confidence and a person's private medical history are two examples.
A gap held briefly, with a plan to close it when the timing is right. One example is waiting for test results before telling the family. That is a delay, not a concealment.
Context can be missing because the speaker never had it, which is a gap and not a filter.
Sharing what you know as you learn it, over several conversations, is different from choosing in advance which facts another person gets.
A short summary that drops detail for length and would readily expand if asked.
this_may_be_it_when: The missing detail is exactly the one that would have changed your decision.
The person knew the fact at the time, and a record or a third party shows it.
Direct questions on the topic get answers that are accurate but still go around it.
Earlier accounts from them have a similar shape: the favorable parts in, the complicating ones out.
When the fact comes out, the first response defends the omission ('you didn't ask') rather than addressing the fact.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They tell you the missing piece as soon as they realize it matters.
They did not know it themselves until recently.
The omitted matter is truly theirs, or a third party's, to keep private, and does not affect your decision.
They volunteered a bigger and uncomfortable fact just before, which does not fit a filter.
When asked directly, they answer directly.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People forget to mention things all the time, especially when busy or anxious.
Some find it hard to share bad news and put it off until they have the words.
Families and workplaces differ in what gets passed on and who is thought to need to know.
A person may believe the information was already known to you.
common_false_positives: A planner of a surprise party who keeps one fact back until the day.
A colleague who did not mention a change because the notice went to everyone.
A clinician, lawyer or counselor bound by confidentiality who cannot tell you.
discernment_questions: Would knowing the missing piece have changed a choice I made?
Did the person have the information when we last spoke about this?
Is the information theirs to withhold, or does it affect me?
Was it shared voluntarily once it mattered, or only after I found it?
Do the things left out tend to be the ones that would change outcomes?
If I ask directly now, what do I get?
less_concerning_if: The missing piece was small and had no bearing on any choice you made.
They fill the gap quickly when asked and say how it was missed.
It happened during a hectic period and has not repeated.
more_concerning_if: The missing information involves money, health, safety, children or legal matters.
You are told the omission was your fault for not asking the right question.
Others in your circle turn out to have known what you were not told.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to ask 'is there anything else I should know?' before every decision.
You regularly learn big facts secondhand.
Your picture of events keeps getting corrected by later discoveries.
You cross-check what they say against other sources, and feel uneasy doing it.
Lying by Omission.repair_check: Mending it means the person hands over the whole picture, including what they knew and when, without being asked twice. They then volunteer things before they are discovered. A version that supplies the missing fact but blames you for not asking leaves the habit in place.
Lying by Omission.boundary_respect_check: Tell them in plain terms what you need to know in order to decide, then watch the next few weeks. Do the facts that matter reach you first, or do you still hear them from other people? The gap between what is promised and what arrives is your answer.
Lying by Omission.psychological_mechanism: We build decisions on what we believe is the whole story. We trust that a person would speak up if something important were missing. A gap in the account is invisible from the inside, so the listener fills it with the most ordinary assumption. Once the omission is found, a person may be told that nothing false was said. That can lead them to doubt their own judgment or their memory of what they were told.
Lying by Omission.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some feel foolish and then betrayed when they find out, even though no lie can be quoted. They may go over old conversations looking for what they missed. They may hesitate to trust good news, or ask so many questions that they sound like an interrogator. Some doubt their memory of what they were told.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the open question in a neutral voice. You could say: 'Is there anything about this that I'd want to know before I decide?' It makes it easy to add the missing piece without anyone feeling accused.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say what you need in order to trust the account. For example: 'If something affects my decision, I need to hear it from you before I find it out myself.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not decide anything large on this person's account alone. Get the key facts from the document, the records or a third person, and hold off until you have them.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe what you were told, and what you later found, to someone not involved. Ask whether the missing piece would have changed their decision. This helps separate fair upset from self-blame.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for decisions, terms and changes in writing, and include the line 'Is there anything else that affects this?' in the message. Keep the reply as a record of what you were told and when.

Lying by Omission.boundary_script: "I'm not saying anything you told me was false. What I found out later changes how I see it, and I would have decided differently. From here, I need to hear anything that affects me from you, first and plainly."
Lying by Omission.safety_note: Usually this is a trust problem and not a danger. That changes if the hidden matter is a debt in your name, a health risk such as an infection, or a legal case. It also changes if it concerns where children or money are, or if asking is met with anger. Then get documents and records from the source and talk to a lawyer, doctor or financial counselor before acting on the person's account.
misuse_warning: If every unmentioned detail counts as a lie, privacy and forgetfulness become charges. The label fits only when the gap mattered to a decision and the other person knew about it.
People are entitled to keep some things to themselves. 'You didn't tell me' is not always a complaint the other person owes an answer to.
Lying by Omission.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying states something false, while omission states only true things. Strategic Incompleteness gives you just enough to act on and keeps you coming back for the rest. The gap is ongoing and builds dependence. Here the gap is a hidden piece in an otherwise finished account. Countering flatly contradicts your version of events, whereas omission contradicts nothing and leaves your picture incomplete.
